purpose: Olaparib is used to treat certain types of cancer, including ovarian, breast, pancreatic, and prostate cancers. It is especially used in people whose cancer is linked to changes in the BRCA gene. Your doctor may use it as a main treatment or to help keep cancer from coming back after chemotherapy.
how_it_works: Cancer cells with certain gene changes, like BRCA mutations, already have trouble repairing their own DNA. Olaparib blocks a protein called PARP that cancer cells rely on to fix that DNA damage. Without PARP, the cancer cells cannot repair themselves and they die off, while healthy cells are less affected.
common_side_effects: Feeling tired or weak, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea or constipation, loss of appetite, headache, low blood cell counts (which can cause anemia, increased risk of infections, or easy bruising and bleeding), and dizziness.
warnings: Olaparib can lower your blood counts significantly, so regular blood tests are important. Rarely, it can cause a serious blood cancer called MDS or AML — tell your doctor right away if you feel very tired or have unusual bruising or bleeding. It can harm an unborn baby, so do not get pregnant or father a child during treatment. Avoid grapefruit and certain medications that can interact with it. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 300 mg (two 150 mg tablets) taken by mouth twice a day, morning and evening, with or without food. Try to take it at the same times each day. Swallow the tablets whole — do not crush or chew them. If you miss a dose, skip it and take your next dose as scheduled.
